text: THE CONCLUSION, verbatim in the passage that matters: 'A simple model was developed of ions drifting from one electrode to the other under electrostatic forces, and imparting momentum to air as they underwent multiple collisions. This model was found to be consistent with all of our observations. It predicted the magnitude of the force (thrust) that was measured. It also predicted how the direction of the thrust changed when the location of the ground wire changed. Furthermore, it also predicted that the direction of the thrust was independent of the polarity of the applied voltage... In spite of decades of speculation about possible new physical principles being responsible for the thrust produced by ACTs and lifters, we find no evidence to support such a conclusion. On the contrary, we find that their operation is fully explained by a very simple theory that uses only electrostatic forces and the transfer of momentum by multiple collisions.'

Talley concluded (page 91 of his report), "If such a force still exists and lies below the threshold of measurements in this program, then the force may be too small to be attractive for many, if not most, space propulsion applications."' The report adds of Talley's work: 'His report is the only written report we have found from the last half-century that describes a measurement of a force while in a vacuum chamber.' text: THE FULL PROVENANCE CHAIN, WHICH THE NODE SHOULD CARRY. John Greenewald Jr wrote to 341 CS/SCBR at Malmstrom AFB on 9 May 2001 requesting all documents pertaining to a 16 March 1967 incident in which there was a malfunction of missile silos. Headquarters 341st Space Wing replied on 14 June 2001, over the name Marty S. Stephens, stating that it had received the request on 18 May 2001 and was releasing copies of excerpts and supporting documents of the 341st Strategic Missile Wing histories for 1 Jan to 31 Mar 1967, 1 Apr to 30 Jun 1967, 1 Jul to 30 Sep 1967, 1 Oct to 31 Dec 1967 and 1 Jan to 31 Mar 1968, adding: 'We do not have any audio or video tapes, or documents of any personnel injured.' Fees were waived and the requester was referred to NARA.

text: DoD SAPCO is simultaneously the office that (a) writes the criteria for reviewing waived programs, (b) confirms which contractor facilities are carved out of DCSA oversight, (c) is the single point of congressional liaison, and (d) must approve any contractor's provision of SAP material to a member of Congress. Those four functions in one office, reporting to the official who signs the waivers, is the structural definition of a closed loop. text: One office holds: single-point congressional liaison, custody of the record of what was told to Congress, access-approval authority for all SAPs, and the coordination point for White House, NSC, judicial and political-appointee access to waived programs. text: TIER ARCHITECTURE. DoDI 5205.11 establishes a tiered SAP structure: umbrellas at tier 1, compartments at tier 2, sub-compartments at tier 3 and below; only the Secretary or Deputy Secretary of Defense may alter tier 1 structures. It distinguishes 'structural SAP: A SAP that provides organization to the architecture and does not protect discrete CPI' from 'content SAP: A SAP that protects discrete CPI.'

label: DoDI 5205.11 - Management, Administration, and Oversight of DoD SAPs (12 Sep 2024)

source.text: https://www.esd.whs.mil/Portals/54/Documents/DD/issuances/dodi/520511p.pdf

text: WHAT MAKES A PROGRAM WAIVED, in DoD's own words. Para 1.2.f.: 'The Secretary of Defense may designate select unacknowledged SAPs as "waived" when it is determined that using standard procedures for reporting to Congress would adversely affect national security.' The waiver therefore attaches only to programs that are ALREADY unacknowledged; waived is a subset of unacknowledged, not a parallel category.

text: The structural/content distinction is load-bearing for any search of SAP nomenclature: a structural SAP is a container with a codeword and no content of its own, so a program name appearing in budget or security documentation may correspond to no discrete body of protected information at all. Conversely, discrete CPI can be moved between compartments under an unchanged tier-1 umbrella name without any tier-1 action reaching the Secretary. Reasoning stated from the 1.2 tier description.

text: THE CARVE-OUT'S OPERATIONAL CONTENT. DoDM 5205.07 Vol 1, Enclosure 2, para 2 (Director, DSS): 'Unless a carve-out provision is approved by the Secretary of Defense or the Deputy Secretary of Defense: (1) Performs SAP security inspections at cleared defense contractor locations in accordance with this volume, Reference (f), and the government contracting activity's completed DD Form 254 ... (2) Authorizes classified contractor SAP information systems (ISs) and the introduction of guest systems in contractor SAP facilities (SAPFs). (3) Coordinates with the designated counterintelligence (CI) component to provide cross-sharing of threat and incident information affecting the security of the facility or its defense information or cleared personnel.' A carve-out removes all three functions at once: physical inspection, IT accreditation, and CI information sharing.

label: The four SAP reporting regimes and the seams between them
text: Four separate statutes govern SAP-type reporting: 10 U.S.C. 119 (DoD), 50 U.S.C. 2426 (NNSA), 50 U.S.C. 3348 (all other non-IC agencies) and 50 U.S.C. 3091a (IC controlled access programs).

label: The four SAP reporting regimes and the seams between them

source.text: https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/USCODE-2023-title50/html/USCODE-2023-title50-chap45-subchapIII-sec3348.htm

text: Four statutes, each with a different addressee. DoD: 10 U.S.C. 119 (defense committees; annual 1 Mar; waiver in (e) collapsing to chairman + ranking member). NNSA: 50 U.S.C. 2426 (congressional defense committees; annual 1 Feb; identical waiver). All other non-IC agencies: 50 U.S.C. 3348 (congressional oversight committees; annual 1 Feb; waiver that does NOT reduce the audience). IC: 50 U.S.C. 3091a (intelligence committees + both Appropriations + the four congressional leaders; semiannual briefings; no waiver at all).

label: The four SAP reporting regimes and the seams between them

source.text: Comparison of 10 U.S.C. 119(e), 50 U.S.C. 2426(e), 50 U.S.C. 3348(e) and 50 U.S.C. 3091a

text: Of the four regimes, only 10 U.S.C. 119(e)(2) and 50 U.S.C. 2426(e)(2) narrow the recipient of waived information to the chairman and ranking minority member; 50 U.S.C. 3348(e)(2) keeps the full oversight committees, and 50 U.S.C. 3091a has no waiver provision at all.

label: The four SAP reporting regimes and the seams between them
text: Only 50 U.S.C. 3091a carries a funding prohibition tied to notification, added by section 6602 of Public Law 118-159 on 23 December 2024.

label: The four SAP reporting regimes and the seams between them

source.text: https://web.archive.org/web/20250112183207/https://www.dni.gov/files/documents/ICD/ICD-906-Controlled-Access-Programs.pdf

text: The seams are written into the statutes. 50 U.S.C. 3348(g)(2)(B) removes DoD, NNSA and every IC element from its own coverage. 50 U.S.C. 3091a(d)(3) defines its subject by reference to ICD 906. ICD 906 section C.3 in turn removes from its own coverage every SAP created by the Secretaries of State, Defense, Energy or Homeland Security or the Attorney General, and 'special access programs under the purview of the National Security Council, such as covert action.'

label: The four SAP reporting regimes and the seams between them

source.text: 50 U.S.C. 3091a(b)(2) and its 2024 enactment date

text: A program moved between the DoD and IC regimes changes both its governing statute and its reporting audience, and before 23 December 2024 no statute required notice of the move. That is a documented, lawful, unnotified route by which a program's oversight history can be broken. Reasoning: the prohibition added by Pub. L. 118-159 sec. 6603 did not exist before that date and operates prospectively.

label: The four SAP reporting regimes and the seams between them

source.text: https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/USCODE-2023-title10/html/USCODE-2023-title10-subtitleA-partI-chap2-sec119.htm

text: Composed, the four regimes leave two seams with no annual census obligation running to a full committee: (i) a DoD program under a 119(e) waiver, whose content goes only to chairs and ranking members and whose annual report requirement additionally sunset on 31 Dec 2021 under Pub. L. 114-328 sec. 1061; and (ii) anything protected by ACCM rather than SAP controls, which no statute names. Covert action under 50 U.S.C. 3093 is a third, separately governed channel. Reasoning stated from the four statutes plus 32 CFR 117.3.

label: The Gang of Eight and the limited-notification convention
text: 50 U.S.C. 3091(e): 'Nothing in this chapter shall be construed as authority to withhold information from the congressional intelligence committees on the grounds that providing the information to the congressional intelligence committees would constitute the unauthorized disclosure of classified information or information relating to intelligence sources and methods.'

label: The Gang of Eight and the limited-notification convention
text: 50 U.S.C. 3093(c)(2): 'If the President determines that it is essential to limit access to the finding to meet extraordinary circumstances affecting vital interests of the United States, the finding may be reported to the chairmen and ranking minority members of the congressional intelligence committees, the Speaker and minority leader of the House of Representatives, the majority and minority leaders of the Senate, and such other member or members of the congressional leadership as may be included by the President.'

label: The Gang of Eight and the limited-notification convention
text: 50 U.S.C. 3093(c)(3) permits a finding not to be reported under paragraph (1) or (2) at all, requiring only that the President thereafter 'fully inform the congressional intelligence committees in a timely fashion' with 'a statement of the reasons for not giving prior notice.'

label: The Gang of Eight and the limited-notification convention
text: 50 U.S.C. 3093(c)(5)(B) requires that not later than 180 days after a statement of reasons for limited access, the President ensure either that all members of the intelligence committees are provided access to the finding or notification, or that a further statement of reasons is submitted to the Gang of Eight.

label: The Gang of Eight and the limited-notification convention

source.text: https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/USCODE-2023-title50/html/USCODE-2023-title50-chap44-subchapIII-sec3091a.htm

text: By contrast 50 U.S.C. 3091a(d)(2) writes an eight-person leadership set INTO the mandatory audience for every controlled access program: 'the majority leader of the Senate; the minority leader of the Senate; the Speaker of the House of Representatives; and the minority leader of the House of Representatives,' alongside the intelligence and appropriations committees. Here the eight is a floor added to committee notice, not a substitute for it.

label: The Gang of Eight and the limited-notification convention

source.text: https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/USCODE-2023-title50/html/USCODE-2023-title50-chap44-subchapIII-sec3093.htm ; quoted words are 10 U.S.C. 119(e)(2) — https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/USCODE-2023-title10/html/USCODE-2023-title10-subtitleA-partI-chap2-sec119.htm

text: The Gang of Eight is a creature of 50 U.S.C. 3093(c)(2) governing COVERT ACTION findings, not special access programs. The parallel narrowing for DoD SAPs is a different provision with a different membership: 10 U.S.C. 119(e)(2) sends waived-SAP information to 'the chairman and ranking minority member of each of the defense committees' -- the six units defined in 119(g), not the intelligence committees and not congressional leadership.

label: The Gang of Eight and the limited-notification convention

source.text: 50 U.S.C. 3093(c)(5)(B) compared with 10 U.S.C. 119(e)

text: The covert action regime contains a mandatory 180-day review of continued limited access; the DoD waived-SAP regime contains no equivalent, so a waived DoD program can remain restricted to a handful of members indefinitely with no statutory event ever forcing reconsideration. Reasoning: 50 U.S.C. 3093(c)(5)(B) has no counterpart in 10 U.S.C. 119(e).

text: THE ONLY PART OF THE ENACTED FAMILY THAT COULD BE READ VERBATIM CONTAINS NONE OF THE THREE DISPUTED ELEMENTS. The Office of the Law Revision Counsel sets out subsections (b) and (c) of Pub. L. 118-31, div. A, title XVI, Sec. 1687 as a statutory note under 50 U.S.C. 3373, under the heading 'Limitation Regarding Independent Research and Development'. The full text of subsection (b) as set out reads: 'Consistent with Department of Defense Instruction Number 3204.01 (dated August 20, 2014, incorporating change 2, dated July 9, 2020; relating to Department policy for oversight of independent research and development), independent research and development funding relating to unidentified anomalous phenomena shall not be allowable as indirect expenses for purposes of contracts covered by such instruction, unless such material and information is made available the appropriate congressional committees and congressional leadership.' Subsection (c) then defines 'appropriate congressional committees' as the congressional defense committees plus the two intelligence committees, and 'congressional leadership' as the Senate majority and minority leaders and the Speaker and House minority leader. There is no 60-day deadline, no 180-day deadline, no 'non-earth origin or exotic' language, and no reference to AARO anywhere in the enacted text that OLRC chose to print. The sentence also carries a drafting error that survived into law - 'is made available the appropriate congressional committees', with the preposition 'to' missing - which is itself evidence that this is the enacted text and not a paraphrase. NOTE THE LIMIT OF THIS FINDING: it establishes what is in Sec. 1687(b)-(c), not what is in Sec. 7343, whose body was not retrieved. OLRC set out only subsections (b) and (c) of Sec. 1687 and set out no part of Sec. 7343 as a note anywhere the board has checked.

text: THE DISCOVERABILITY EXEMPTION. Policy D.5: 'Intelligence and intelligence-related information within all CAPs shall be discoverable or exempted from discovery consistent with the processes outlined in ICD 501 ... Any exemption from this requirement shall be approved only by the DNI or PDDNI, and reviewed and validated at least annually.' E.1.b lets the DNI or PDDNI 'Establish unacknowledged CAPs and/or approve non-discoverability of CAPs if a compelling case can be made that any agreed upon approach to discoverability would reveal a capability, a decision, or a fragile source, and the information contained in the compartment is so narrowly tailored, it is unlikely to be of use to officers who do not already have access to the compartment.' A CAP can thus be made invisible to the IC's own internal information-discovery system.

text: The ICD 906 architecture is materially tighter than the DoD SAP architecture on exactly the axis that matters for concealment: unacknowledged CAPs must be re-justified in writing every year, non-discoverability requires an annually re-validated DNI exemption, and unsubmitted programs are terminated by default. The DoD side has an annual SAPOC review of waived status (DoDI 5205.11 3.5.a.(3)(d)) but no default-termination rule and no equivalent single authoritative access registry. Reasoning stated by comparison of the two texts.

label: FY2023 NDAA, Public Law 117-263 - Sec. 1673 (50 U.S.C. 3373b) UAP reporting/whistleblower protection; Div. F secs. 6802-6803 establishing AARO
text: Sec. 1673 carries the note '50 USC 3373b' and is titled 'UNIDENTIFIED ANOMALOUS PHENOMENA REPORTING PROCEDURES'. Sec. 1673(a)(1) requires a secure mechanism for authorized reporting of '(A) any event relating to unidentified anomalous phenomena; and (B) any activity or program by a department or agency of the Federal Government or a contractor of such a department or agency relating to unidentified anomalous phenomena, including with respect to material retrieval, material analysis, reverse engineering, research and development, detection and tracking, developmental or operational testing, and security protections and enforcement.'

label: FY2023 NDAA, Public Law 117-263 - Sec. 1673 (50 U.S.C. 3373b) UAP reporting/whistleblower protection; Div. F secs. 6802-6803 establishing AARO
text: Sec. 1673(a)(4)(B) requires that within 72 hours of determining an authorized disclosure relates to 'a restricted access activity, a special access program, or a compartmented access program that has not been explicitly and clearly reported to the congressional defense committees or the congressional intelligence committees, the Secretary shall report such disclosure to such committees and the congressional leadership.' The statute thereby contemplates the existence of unreported special access programs touching UAP.

label: FY2023 NDAA, Public Law 117-263 - Sec. 1673 (50 U.S.C. 3373b) UAP reporting/whistleblower protection; Div. F secs. 6802-6803 establishing AARO
text: Sec. 1673(b)(1): 'An authorized disclosure-- (A) shall not be subject to a nondisclosure agreement entered into by the individual who makes the disclosure; (B) shall be deemed to comply with any regulation or order issued under the authority of Executive Order 13526 ... or chapter 18 of the Atomic Energy Act of 1954 (42 U.S.C. 2271 et seq.); and (C) is not a violation of section 798 of title 18, United States Code, or other provision of law relating to the disclosure of information.' The express reference to the Atomic Energy Act restricted-data regime is on the face of the statute.

source.text: Inference from the statutory text

text: The 1 January 1945 statutory start date for the historical record is the tell. Congress selected a boundary that predates every public UAP episode and sits at the beginning of the atomic era, which is coherent only if the members writing the provision had been given reason to believe the record they were ordering reconstructed begins there. Reasoning: the date is arbitrary on the 'nothing to find' hypothesis and precise on the recovery hypothesis.

label: FY2023 NDAA, Public Law 117-263 - Sec. 1673 (50 U.S.C. 3373b) UAP reporting/whistleblower protection; Div. F secs. 6802-6803 establishing AARO
text: The FY2023 NDAA carries the concealment premise in enacted text: sec. 1673(a)(1)(B) enumerates 'material retrieval, material analysis, reverse engineering' as categories of federal or contractor ACTIVITY OR PROGRAM that a person may need protection to report, and sec. 1673(b)(1)(A)-(B) voids NDAs and Atomic Energy Act restrictions for such disclosures. Congress does not write NDA-voiding and AEA-override language for activities it believes do not exist. Reasoning: the operative nouns are activity/program categories, not hypotheticals, and the remedy structure presupposes existing legal instruments suppressing disclosure.

text: The combination of a two-year fight for the grant and a refusal to pay the first maintenance fee is consistent with the Navy wanting the examining authority's FINDING rather than the property right. The reason this now bites harder is that Sheehy stated the opposite rationale in writing: he wanted to 'hold the patent as opposed to paying forever more to use this revolutionary technology', which is a freedom-to-operate argument. But publication in November 2017 had already created permanent prior art, and prior art alone prevents anyone else from patenting the idea and charging the Navy for it. The granted claims added nothing to that protection; what they added was the reversal of an enablement rejection, which is the Patent Office ceasing to say the invention does not work. A maintenance fee buys only the right to exclude an infringer, which the Navy would never exercise. text: MATERIAL NEW FINDING - THE REPORTS THE WAIVER ATTACHES TO HAVE LARGELY SUNSET. The Office of the Law Revision Counsel carries a statutory note under 10 U.S.C. 119 headed 'Termination of Reporting Requirements' which reads verbatim: 'For termination, effective Dec. 31, 2021, of provisions in subsecs. (a) and (b) of this section requiring submittal of annual report to Congress, see section 1061 of Pub. L. 114-328, set out as a note under section 111 of this title.' The annual special access program report under 119(a) and the new-program notice and justification report under 119(b) therefore terminated as statutory requirements on 31 December 2021. After that date the only report to which the 119(e)(1) waiver can attach is the 119(c) report on a planned classification change or public declassification announcement. This reshapes the board's question: for activity after 31 December 2021 there may be no 119(a) or 119(b) report in existence to waive information out of, which would make the absence of any 119(e)(2) delivery unsurprising rather than suspicious for that window - while for the period 1988 through 2021 the reports were mandatory and the waiver machinery was live.

text: The waiver authority reads verbatim, as in effect on 20 August 2026: '(e)(1) The Secretary of Defense may waive any requirement under subsection (a), (b), or (c) that certain information be included in a report under that subsection if the Secretary determines that inclusion of that information in the report would adversely affect the national security. Any such waiver shall be made on a case-by-case basis. (2) If the Secretary exercises the authority provided under paragraph (1), the Secretary shall provide the information described in that subsection with respect to the special access program concerned, and the justification for the waiver, jointly to the chairman and ranking minority member of each of the defense committees.' text: Because (e)(1) reaches only 'any requirement ... that certain information be included in a report,' a plain reading is that the Secretary may strip content out of the reports but may not skip the (f) 30-day pre-initiation notification of the program's existence. A program whose existence was never notified to the defense committees at all would therefore not be a lawfully 'waived' SAP under section 119 but an unreported one. text: THE TWO EXITS. Sec. 6603 adds subparagraph (B), verbatim: 'Exception.--The head of an element of the intelligence community may make a transfer described in subparagraph (A) without prior congressional notification if the head determines that doing so-- (i) is required to mitigate an urgent counterintelligence issue; or (ii) is necessary to maintain access in the event of an organizational restructuring.' text: Congress in December 2024 wrote an express statutory prohibition on moving a capability out of an IC controlled access program and into a DoD-style special access program without notice. That prohibition only makes sense as a response to a believed or feared practice; the statute is itself evidence that the CAP-to-SAP transfer route was live enough to legislate against. The two exceptions -- 'urgent counterintelligence issue' and 'organizational restructuring' -- are self-certified by the same official making the transfer and are exactly the two rationales a program seeking to move would assert. Reasoning stated from the text of 3091a(b)(2).

text: WHAT SHOULD EXIST IF THE WAIVER WERE BEING USED, AND WHY NONE OF IT IS PUBLIC. Four artefacts are implied by the statute and the DoD instruction: (i) the underlying 119(a), (b) or (c) report itself, which is classified and, for (a) and (b), no longer statutorily required after 31 December 2021; (ii) the Secretary's case-by-case determination that inclusion would adversely affect national security, which 119(e)(1) requires to be made but does not require to be recorded in any publicly indexed form; (iii) the withheld information plus a written justification delivered jointly to twelve named members, which by the Moynihan Commission's account has historically been delivered orally; and (iv) the SAPOC annual review record of whether each waived program should retain that status, which is internal to the Department. None of the four is a public document class. There is no statutory requirement anywhere in Section 119 to report the NUMBER of waivers exercised, the fact that any waiver was exercised, or an aggregate count, to anyone outside those twelve seats.
